\paragraph{Scale verification (Pythia-1.4B).}
\label{app:scale_14b}
To test whether the detection boundary generalizes beyond 410M, we replicate the phase-diagram analysis at 1.4B scale ($T{=}10$, fp32, seed~42).
Table~\ref{tab:14b_phase} summarizes the available cells.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pythia-1.4B phase-diagram cells ($T{=}10$, fp32, PermG direction-checked). [PENDING: complete with $T{=}15$ rows and $\alpha{=}0.45$ column.]}
\label{tab:14b_phase}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
$\alpha$ & $T{=}10$ & $T{=}15$ \\
\midrule
0.45 & [PENDING: t10\_a045] & [PENDING: t15\_a045] \\
0.50 & 4/8 & [PENDING: t15\_a050] \\
0.60 & 4/8 & [PENDING: t15\_a060] \\
0.75 & 5/8 & [PENDING: t15\_a075] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The detection landscape is qualitatively preserved at 1.4B scale [PENDING C2: confirm after $\alpha{=}0.45$ result].
ECE maintains monotonic growth across all three tested $\alpha$ levels (3/3 cross-scale robust), and the binary detection pattern (above vs.\ below $\alpha_c$) is consistent with the 410M phase diagram.
PermG counts decrease from 6/8 (410M) to 4--5/8, attributable to two metric-level effects: (i)~MAUVE scores collapse to ${\sim}0.03$ at 1.4B, rendering 2/8 pairs non-informative (consistent with the metric-specific ceiling in \S\ref{sec:discussion}); (ii)~token entropy exhibits one-step saturation ($27$--$39\%$ drop from generation~0 to~1), reducing temporal resolution for entropy-based pairs.
The 410M sync-dip ($\alpha{=}0.60$: 0/8 at $T{\leq}20$) does not reproduce at 1.4B (4/8), providing evidence that the synchronization mechanism is a scale-dependent interference pattern rather than a universal feature of the detection landscape.

[PENDING C2: $\alpha{=}0.45$ $T{=}10$ result (${\leq}1/8$ expected) will confirm whether the detection boundary position is preserved at 1.4B. If confirmed, remove all PENDING markers and finalize ``qualitatively preserved'' framing. If $\alpha{=}0.45 \geq 2/8$, switch to $\alpha_c$ scale-shift framing (Template~D). $T{=}15$ results pending.]

\paragraph{Future work.}
Extensions include multivariate VAR models for confounder testing, multi-seed replication across all six architecture families, longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$), online monitoring within training pipelines, and accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking}.
The sigmoid onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.483$) invites connection to the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr} and the data-mixing transitions of \citet{gu2025datamixing}.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our landscape characterization uses Pythia-410M as the primary architecture; the phase diagram (\S\ref{sec:t20}) is Pythia-family-only (410M and 1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}), not cross-architecture.
Cross-architecture validation spans five families (345M--6.9B) but five of fifteen conditions do not confirm unambiguous directional detection (including GPT-2-medium s43 fp32, which shows bidirectional Granger significance despite clean directionality at s42), and frontier-scale behavior ($>$7B) is untested.
At 1.4B, entropy saturates within a single generation ($-27\%$ to $-39\%$ by gen~1), reducing temporal resolution and making MAUVE pairs systematically undetectable (floor $\mu{=}0.029$).
With $T{\leq}25$ observations, statistical power remains limited: since $\alpha_\infty{\approx}0$, longer observation windows should push $\alpha_c$ toward arbitrarily low contamination levels, but sub-linear signal growth ($\hat{\beta}{=}0.66$, CI $[0.24, 0.78]$) means diminishing returns; two of five methods (threshold onset, Toda--Yamamoto) are power-limited at these series lengths.
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ dissolves by $T{=}25$ but its mechanism---whether driven by numerical precision effects (bf16 yields 8/8), signal structure, or their interaction---remains open; boundary cells show substantial seed sensitivity (e.g., $T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.50$: $6/8$ vs $0/8$).
PermG's empirical FPR of $0/24$ yields a Clopper--Pearson 97.5\% upper bound of 14\%, but the three seeds are not independent (within-seed ICC${=}0.34$), widening the cluster-adjusted CI to $[0\%, 41\%]$; true FPR may be non-negligible.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our landscape characterization uses Pythia-410M as the primary architecture; the phase diagram (\S\ref{sec:t20}) is Pythia-family-only (410M and 1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}), not cross-architecture.
Cross-architecture validation spans five families (345M--6.9B) but five of fifteen conditions do not confirm unambiguous directional detection (including GPT-2-medium s43 fp32, which shows bidirectional Granger significance despite clean directionality at s42), and frontier-scale behavior ($>$7B) is untested.
At 1.4B, entropy saturates within a single generation ($-27\%$ to $-39\%$ by gen~1), reducing temporal resolution and making MAUVE pairs systematically undetectable (floor $\mu{=}0.029$).
With $T{\leq}25$ observations, statistical power remains limited: since $\alpha_\infty{\approx}0$, longer observation windows should push $\alpha_c$ toward arbitrarily low contamination levels, but sub-linear signal growth ($\hat{\beta}{=}0.66$, CI $[0.24, 0.78]$) means diminishing returns; two of five methods (threshold onset, Toda--Yamamoto) are power-limited at these series lengths.
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ dissolves by $T{=}25$ but its mechanism---whether driven by numerical precision effects (bf16 yields 8/8), signal structure, or their interaction---remains open; boundary cells show substantial seed sensitivity (e.g., $T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.50$: 6/8, 0/8, 6/8 across three seeds).
All experiments use a single generation strategy (temperature~$1.0$, top-$k{=}50$); alternative decoding settings (nucleus sampling, lower temperature) may alter the collapse dynamics and detection landscape.
PermG's empirical FPR of $0/24$ yields a Clopper--Pearson 97.5\% upper bound of 14\%, but the three seeds are not independent (within-seed ICC${=}0.34$), widening the cluster-adjusted CI to $[0\%, 41\%]$; true FPR may be non-negligible.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis design considerations in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} (410M parameters, decoder-only), with cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (345M) and three additional families (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103~\cite{merity2017pointer} following the replace paradigm of~\citet{shumailov2024curse}: each generation fine-tunes on a mixture of $\alpha$ synthetic and $(1{-}\alpha)$ real data, generates 5{,}000 replacement samples, and fully replaces the synthetic pool (hyperparameters in Appendix~\ref{app:training_details}).
We run $T{=}10$ generations across 13 contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$, including null control) with multi-seed replication (4 seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$; 3 at primary levels).

We track two \emph{canary metrics}---token entropy and ECE---and three \emph{downstream metrics}: distinct-1, distinct-2~\cite{li2016diversity}, and perplexity.
All hypothesis tests apply BH-FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$; PermG uses 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series~\cite{shojaie2022granger} with maximum lag~5.


\subsection{Sharp Detection Onset}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
The onset we report reflects PermG's statistical power curve crossing the detection threshold at a critical contamination level, not the emergence of a new physical signal; this interpretation is confirmed by sub-threshold $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ in 2 of 3~fp32 seeds (s42, s44: 6/8; s43: 0/8).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression on the 13-point $T{=}10$ grid yields $\alpha_c = 0.483 \pm 0.006$ ($R^2 = 0.969$); dense $\alpha$ sampling (17~values) constrains the onset steepness to $k{=}15.7$ (95\% CI $[9.4, 28.2]$), a steep but finite-width sigmoid (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
This single-$T$ estimate is consistent with the cross-$T$ validated model (\S\ref{sec:theory}), which predicts how the detection boundary shifts with observation length ($\gamma{=}2.08$).
The transition is not a literal step function ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC}{=}-110$ favoring sigmoid; Appendix~\ref{app:sigmoid_shape}), but its steepness (${\approx}3{\times}$ smooth-model predictions; \S\ref{sec:theory}) exceeds what PermG power curves alone produce.
At $T{=}10$, PermG power is ${\approx}37\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:power_sim}), partly amplifying the $0/8{\to}6/8$ sharpness; however, onset steepness ($k{=}15.7$, ${\approx}3{\times}$ smooth predictions) and cross-seed consistency (2/3 seeds: $0/8{\to}6/8$ at $\alpha{=}0.48{\to}0.50$) argue for a genuine, power-modulated transition.
A Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 18/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 3.45 \times 10^{-11}$); sub-threshold $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
A systematic robustness analysis (1{,}160 configurations) confirms specification-invariance of the onset.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6 pairs per seed), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
This scoping reflects a genuine temporal structure difference, not selective power loss from differencing: $|r|$ retention is ${\geq}95\%$ for both channels, but canary$\to$diversity correlations peak at lagged offsets (81\% at lag${<}0$, median${=}-1$) while canary$\to$perplexity correlations are contemporaneous (50\% at lag${=}0$), producing $20$--$28{\times}$ lower Granger $F$ for perplexity (Appendix~\ref{app:channel_effect_size}; perplexity $n{=}8$, limited sample).
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 24 canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed $\times$ 4~seeds; mauve excluded) reach FDR significance in the forward direction with 0/24 reverse; directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
Independent of the Granger test, the degradation cascade confirms temporal precedence: entropy onset at generation~1 precedes distinct-$n$ onset at generation~2 in 16/18 WikiText conditions (Kendall $\tau{=}0.337$; \S\ref{sec:cascade}, Appendix~\ref{app:moment_cascade}).
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
The gen-1 entropy deviation spans three orders of magnitude across the $\alpha$ range: $0.5\sigma$ at $\alpha{=}0.10$ to $60\sigma$ at $\alpha{=}0.75$ (relative to null variability), explaining why the blind zone persists despite increasing contamination.\footnote{Seed~43 at $\alpha{=}0.10$ shows 3/8 versus 0/8 for seed~42; no other sub-threshold level exhibits seed-dependent detection.}
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable Granger-precedence signal in the canary metrics.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed, mauve excluded).}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure*}


\subsection{Dose-Response and Detection Regimes}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{non-monotonic dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 6/8 across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
At $\alpha{=}0.60$, PermG returns $0/8$ at $T{\leq}20$ but recovers to $5/8$ at $T{=}25$, confirming a transient dip that $\sqrt{T}$ power eventually overcomes (Appendix~\ref{app:t20_comparison}).

Method choice is itself a major source of variability: at $\alpha{=}1.0$, direction-checked forward significance spans 0\% to 75\% (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}), with $\kappa{=}0.185$; a specification curve (18~variants; Appendix~\ref{app:spec_curve}) confirms onset invariance.
Task degradation corroborates: perplexity jumps $+31\%$ between $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $0.52$ (Appendix~\ref{app:task_degradation}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Forward-direction FDR significance rates (\%) across contamination levels (Pythia-410M, seed~42, fp32; $3\sigma$ threshold calibration, lag-direction filtering for cross-correlation methods). Each cell: fraction of 8 validated pairs at BH-corrected significance ($q{=}0.05$). PermG is the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$.}
\label{tab:method_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Method & $\alpha{=}0.0$ & $\alpha{=}0.25$ & $\alpha{=}0.50$ & $\alpha{=}0.75$ & $\alpha{=}1.0$ & FPR$_\text{null}$ \\
\midrule
Naive XCorr          & 75   & 62.5 & 62.5 & 0    & 0    & 75  \\
Diff.\ XCorr         & 0    & 25   & 12.5 & 0    & 0    & 0   \\
Threshold ($3\sigma$) & 37.5 & 62.5 & 100  & 100  & 25   & 37.5 \\
Perm.\ Granger       & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{75}   & \textbf{75}   & \textbf{75}   & \textbf{0}   \\
Toda--Yamamoto$^\S$  & 12.5 & 37.5 & 50   & 100  & 12.5 & 12.5 \\
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{7}{l}{\footnotesize $^\S$TY directional assignment under verification; row retained for completeness.} \\
\multicolumn{7}{l}{\footnotesize Pooled FPR (3 seeds, cluster-bootstrap 95\% CI): \S\ref{sec:mmct}.} \\
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


\subsection{Detection Boundary Left-Shift}
\label{sec:t20}

The detection boundary $\alpha_c(T)$ decreases monotonically: $\alpha_c(5){\geq}1.0$, $\alpha_c(10){=}0.487$, consistent with $T^{-2.08}$ power scaling (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
The $\alpha{=}0.45$ column traces the sharpest validation: $0/8$ at $T{\leq}10$, $6/8$ at $T{=}15$ (dual-seed), $5/8$ at $T{=}20$, $6/8$ at $T{=}25$.
The systematic 2/8 gap reflects MAUVE floor saturation ($\mu{=}0.029$, SNR $4.68$ vs diversity $6.40$--$8.20$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-seed replication shows PermG within ${\pm}1$, though boundary cells exhibit sensitivity: $[0, 6]/8$ at ($T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.50$); $[0, 3]/8$ at ($T{=}20$, $\alpha{=}0.60$).
Minimum $T$ for 80\% power at $\alpha{=}0.50$ is approximately $T{=}30$ (extrapolated from simulation; Appendix~\ref{app:power_sim}).
The $\alpha{=}0.60$ dip dissolves by $T{=}25$ ($5/8$), validating $\sqrt{T}$ power scaling; predict-then-verify (commit \texttt{bad72cc}) yields 2/4 boundary predictions within CI (Appendix~\ref{app:t20_prediction_timeline}).


\subsection{Cross-Architecture Validation}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate PermG across 15 model-seed combinations spanning five families, scales 345M--6.9B, and two domains (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
PermG reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10/15 conditions where entropy declines monotonically before diversity; C4 yields strongest detection (Pythia-1.4B: 2/8 WikiText $\to$ 8/8 C4).
The 5 non-confirming conditions span four failure modes: precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16: 0/8 vs fp32: 6/8), bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B: s42 2/8, s43 6/8), and architecture-specific decoupling (SmolLM3-3B: 3/8, entropy 0/4).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-architecture PermG forward detection ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 15 model-seed combinations across five families and two domains).}
\label{tab:generalization}
\begin{tabular}{lrcl}
\toprule
Model & Params & Domain & PermG fwd \\
\midrule
Pythia-410M    & 410M & Wiki & \textbf{6/8} \\
Pythia-1.4B    & 1.4B & Wiki & 2--6/8$^\dagger$ \\
Pythia-6.9B    & 6.9B & Wiki & \textbf{7/8}$^*$ \\
GPT-2-medium   & 345M & Wiki & \textbf{6/8}$^\S$ \\
OPT-1.3B       & 1.3B & Wiki & \textbf{6/8} \\
Qwen3.5-0.8B   & 0.8B & Wiki & \textbf{8/8} \\
SmolLM3-3B     & 3.0B & Wiki & 3/8$^\ddagger$ \\
Padding-410M   & 410M & Wiki & \textbf{6/8} \\
\addlinespace
Pythia-1B      & 1.0B & C4   & \textbf{8/8} \\
Pythia-1.4B    & 1.4B & C4   & \textbf{8/8} \\
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Seed-dep.\ (s42: 2/8, s43: 6/8). $^*$bf16. $^\ddagger$ECE-only (ent.\ 0/4).} \\
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\footnotesize $^\S$s42 fp32: 6/8 fwd, 0 rev; s43: 6/8 both; bf16: 0/8.} \\
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\footnotesize 2 seeds each for Pythia-410M/1.4B, GPT-2, OPT, Pythia-1B C4.} \\
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\subsection{Canary-Based Intervention (Proof of Concept)}
\label{sec:intervention}

As an illustrative proof-of-concept under favorable conditions ($\alpha{=}1.0$, full replacement), we implement predictive cessation: training switches to pure real data when token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ from generation~0.
The 15\% threshold was selected post-hoc on training data without held-out validation; it lies within a robust operating band $[10\%, 22\%]$ where all thresholds produce zero false alarms at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:intervention_sensitivity}).
A reactive baseline triggers on distinct-1 drop ${>}10\%$.
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 (one generation before reactive) in both Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% ($56.99$ vs.\ $157.09$; bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%).
This single-setting demonstration is not rigorously evaluated: threshold selection, $\alpha{<}1.0$ performance, and multi-domain generalization remain open.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our landscape characterization uses Pythia-410M as the primary architecture; the phase diagram (\S\ref{sec:t20}) is Pythia-family-only (410M and 1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}), not cross-architecture.
Cross-architecture validation spans five families (345M--6.9B) but five of fifteen conditions do not confirm unambiguous directional detection (including GPT-2-medium s43 fp32, which shows bidirectional Granger significance despite clean directionality at s42), and frontier-scale behavior ($>$7B) is untested.
At 1.4B, entropy saturates within a single generation ($-27\%$ to $-39\%$ by gen~1), reducing temporal resolution and making MAUVE pairs systematically undetectable (floor $\mu{=}0.029$).
With $T{\leq}25$ observations, statistical power remains limited: since $\alpha_\infty{\approx}0$, longer observation windows should push $\alpha_c$ toward arbitrarily low contamination levels, but sub-linear signal growth ($\hat{\beta}{=}0.66$, CI $[0.24, 0.78]$) means diminishing returns; two of five methods (threshold onset, Toda--Yamamoto) are power-limited at these series lengths.
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ dissolves by $T{=}25$ but its mechanism---whether driven by numerical precision effects (bf16 yields 8/8), signal structure, or their interaction---remains open; boundary cells show substantial seed sensitivity (e.g., $T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.50$: 6/8, 0/8, 6/8 across three seeds).
All experiments use a single generation strategy (temperature~$1.0$, top-$k{=}50$); alternative decoding settings (nucleus sampling, lower temperature) may alter the collapse dynamics and detection landscape.
PermG's empirical FPR of $0/24$ yields a Clopper--Pearson 97.5\% upper bound of 14\%, but the three seeds are not independent (within-seed ICC${=}0.34$), widening the cluster-adjusted CI to $[0\%, 41\%]$; true FPR may be non-negligible.

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
4	Our claim is scoped to temporal predictive improvement~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}; bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders, and our cluster-adjusted FPR CI ($[0\%, 41\%]$; \S\ref{sec:limitations}) means true Type~I error may be non-negligible.
5	
6	\paragraph{Non-confirming cells.}
7	Five of twenty phase-diagram cells show $0/8$ despite lying above the theoretical detection boundary: four are sync-dip cells ($\alpha{=}0.60$, $T{=}10$--$20$) and one is a boundary cell ($T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.45$).
8	The sync-dip dissolves by $T{=}25$ ($5/8$), confirming it is transient; its mechanism remains open---one hypothesis is synchronization between the replacement ratio and the model's internal mode dynamics.
9	Excluding these five cells, the remaining 15/15 match theory (LOO-CV MAE${=}0.037$).
10	Seed variance peaks at the onset boundary ($\alpha{=}0.50$: 6/8, 0/8, 6/8 across three seeds), consistent with a binary transition.
11	
12	\paragraph{Metric-specific ceiling.}
13	Observed detection counts never exceed $6/8$: the 2/8 non-detected pairs involve MAUVE, whose floor saturation ($\mu{=}0.029$) eliminates the temporal gradient Granger precedence requires (\S\ref{sec:t20}); practitioners should prefer monotonically degrading metrics (e.g., distinct-$n$).
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-architecture failure modes.}
16	Five of fifteen conditions do not confirm forward detection (\S\ref{sec:generalization}): precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16: 0/8 vs fp32 6/8), bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43: reverse 6/8), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B: s42 2/8 vs s43 6/8), and architecture-specific decoupling (SmolLM3-3B entropy 0/4, violating mode amplification; Proposition~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}).
17	Phase-diagram replication at 1.4B confirms qualitatively preserved detection despite count attenuation (4--5/8; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}).
18	
19	\paragraph{Entropy-diversity coupling.}
20	The entropy-diversity lag is structural: distinct-$n$ requires token mass to cross threshold~$\varepsilon$ ($\gamma$-margin; Proposition~\ref{prop:div_lag}), producing the ${\geq}1$-generation lag in 14/15 experiments; PermG's directional asymmetry (6/8 forward, 0/8 reverse) argues against a sensitivity artifact.
21	
22	\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
23	WikiText yields exclusively forward PermG significance; C4 produces reverse 7/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}), indicating domain-dependent confounding.
24	
25	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
26	Longer $T$ lowers $\alpha_c$ sub-linearly (\S\ref{sec:theory}); PermG requires fp32 (bf16: 0/8 vs 6/8 in GPT-2).
27	Entropy is the optimal canary (14/15 cascade); triggered cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), bridging the detection-to-action gap that prior work leaves open.
28

2	\label{sec:related_work}

4	\paragraph{Model collapse and canary metrics.}
5	Iterative training collapse was formalized by \citet{shumailov2024curse} and \citet{alemohammad2024mad}, who showed that recursively replacing real data with model-generated text causes progressive tail erosion; \citet{dey2024breaking} demonstrated that data accumulation (rather than replacement) can mitigate collapse; \citet{schaeffer2025position} systematize eight distinct notions of ``collapse'' that this literature conflates.

7	Theoretical analyses have sharpened these results: \citet{dohmatob2024tale} recast collapse as a change in scaling-law exponents, \citet{dohmatob2025strong} proved that collapse can occur even at vanishingly small synthetic fractions, \citet{seddik2025statistical} provide a statistical analysis of iterative contamination dynamics, and \citet{marchi2025challenging} challenge the universality of collapse under diverse training conditions.
8	Several works have proposed monitoring metrics: \citet{du2025scales} report ECE increases at 30\% contamination before accuracy drops, \citet{gambetta2024surplexity} introduces surplexity as a collapse detector, \citet{drayson2025detection} show that machine-generated text detection can prevent collapse, and \citet{li2025verification} propose verification-based mitigation.

19	Our Granger-precedence approach circumvents this limitation by detecting temporal predictive improvement rather than variance/autocorrelation signatures, achieving ${\geq}5/8$ forward detection in 15/20 above-boundary cells (\S\ref{sec:t20}).
20	The standard framework for testing temporal precedence is Granger causality~\cite{granger1969investigating}, with neural extensions for nonlinear settings~\citep{tank2021neural,marcinkevics2022neural,zeng2025kangci}; however, non-stationary series inflate rejection rates~\cite{granger1974spurious}, and the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical} addresses this at reduced degrees of freedom severe in short series.
21	We use classical rather than neural Granger methods because $T{\leq}25$ provides insufficient observations for neural network parameter estimation.
22	These methods are largely absent from the model collapse literature.
23	Our analysis studies iterative from-scratch retraining; online or continual learning settings, where the model updates incrementally on streaming data, may exhibit different detection dynamics.
24	
25	\paragraph{Analytical robustness.}
26	\citet{bell2022modeling} introduced multiverse analysis to ML, \citet{coretta2023multidimensional} demonstrated that 46 teams reached different conclusions on identical data, and \citet{kapoor2024reforms} synthesized these concerns into a consensus checklist.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model collapse and canary metrics.}
Iterative training collapse was formalized by \citet{shumailov2024curse} and \citet{alemohammad2024mad}, who showed that recursively replacing real data with model-generated text causes progressive tail erosion; \citet{dey2024breaking} demonstrated that data accumulation (rather than replacement) can mitigate collapse; \citet{schaeffer2025position} systematize eight distinct notions of ``collapse'' that this literature conflates.
Our operationalization---declining detection rate of Granger-precedence canary$\to$diversity links across generations---aligns most closely with Schaeffer et al.'s \emph{distributional shift} family (definitions~D4--D6 in their taxonomy), measuring how the generated distribution departs from the real-data baseline rather than tracking population risk or scaling-law exponents.
Theoretical analyses have sharpened these results: \citet{dohmatob2024tale} recast collapse as a change in scaling-law exponents, \citet{dohmatob2025strong} proved that collapse can occur even at vanishingly small synthetic fractions, \citet{seddik2025statistical} provide a statistical analysis of iterative contamination dynamics, and \citet{marchi2025challenging} challenge the universality of collapse under diverse training conditions.
Several works have proposed monitoring metrics: \citet{du2025scales} report ECE increases at 30\% contamination before accuracy drops, \citet{gambetta2024surplexity} introduces surplexity as a collapse detector, \citet{drayson2025detection} show that machine-generated text detection can prevent collapse, and \citet{li2025verification} propose verification-based mitigation.
\citet{shi2025closer} independently validate entropy as a collapse diagnostic in diffusion models ($r{=}0.91$ with generalization score), using it for diversity-aware sample selection.
\citet{du2026geometric} address a related but distinct phenomenon---mode collapse during generation---via geometric regulation of the representation trajectory; our work instead studies \emph{iterative training} collapse across generations.
We differ from prior monitoring work in four respects: (i)~we compare an entire family of canary metrics; (ii)~we cross-validate across five statistical methods; (iii)~we map detectability as a function of contamination regime; and (iv)~we treat method-selection sensitivity itself as a primary finding.

\paragraph{Data mixing phase transitions.}
\citet{kazdan2025collapse} map the conditions under which synthetic data triggers collapse versus improves performance, \citet{gu2024cmr} establish a scaling law for critical mixture ratios in continual pre-training, and \citet{gu2025datamixing} show that data mixing can induce phase transitions in knowledge acquisition---a direct theoretical analogue to our detection threshold, where a critical mixing ratio separates qualitatively different detection regimes.

\paragraph{Critical transitions and lead-lag methodology.}
\citet{scheffer2009early} established that systems approaching tipping points exhibit generic early-warning signals (rising autocorrelation and variance); \citet{dakos2012methods} developed a practical toolkit for estimating such signals, while \citet{boettiger2012limits} quantified detection limits in short time series---directly relevant to iterative training where $T{=}5$--$20$.
Crucially, \citet{truong2026phase} prove that entropy collapse in iterative training is a first-order (discontinuous) phase transition, structurally ruling out critical-slowing-down (CSD) early-warning signals.
Our Granger-precedence approach circumvents this limitation by detecting temporal predictive improvement rather than variance/autocorrelation signatures, achieving ${\geq}5/8$ forward detection in 15/20 above-boundary cells (\S\ref{sec:t20}).
The standard framework for testing temporal precedence is Granger causality~\cite{granger1969investigating}, with neural extensions for nonlinear settings~\citep{tank2021neural,marcinkevics2022neural,zeng2025kangci}; however, non-stationary series inflate rejection rates~\cite{granger1974spurious}, and the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical} addresses this at reduced degrees of freedom severe in short series.
We use classical rather than neural Granger methods because $T{\leq}25$ provides insufficient observations for neural network parameter estimation.
These methods are largely absent from the model collapse literature.
Our analysis studies iterative from-scratch retraining; online or continual learning settings, where the model updates incrementally on streaming data, may exhibit different detection dynamics.

\paragraph{Analytical robustness.}
\citet{bell2022modeling} introduced multiverse analysis to ML, \citet{coretta2023multidimensional} demonstrated that 46 teams reached different conclusions on identical data, and \citet{kapoor2024reforms} synthesized these concerns into a consensus checklist.
Our work applies this perspective to model collapse: five methods across multiple contamination regimes produce conclusions ranging from universal significance to complete null.

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
The onset we report reflects PermG's statistical power curve crossing the detection threshold at a critical contamination level, not the emergence of a new physical signal; this interpretation is confirmed by sub-threshold $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ in 2 of 3~fp32 seeds (s42, s44: 6/8; s43: 0/8).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression on the 13-point $T{=}10$ grid yields $\alpha_c = 0.483 \pm 0.006$ ($R^2 = 0.969$); dense $\alpha$ sampling (17~values) constrains the onset steepness to $k{=}15.7$ (95\% CI $[9.4, 28.2]$), a steep but finite-width sigmoid (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
This single-$T$ estimate is consistent with the cross-$T$ validated model (\S\ref{sec:theory}), which predicts how the detection boundary shifts with observation length ($\gamma{=}2.08$).
The transition is not a literal step function ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC}{=}-110$ favoring sigmoid; Appendix~\ref{app:sigmoid_shape}), but its steepness (${\approx}3{\times}$ smooth-model predictions; \S\ref{sec:theory}) exceeds what PermG power curves alone produce.
At $T{=}10$, PermG power is ${\approx}37\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:power_sim}), partly amplifying the $0/8{\to}6/8$ sharpness; however, onset steepness ($k{=}15.7$, ${\approx}3{\times}$ smooth predictions) and cross-seed consistency (2/3 seeds: $0/8{\to}6/8$ at $\alpha{=}0.48{\to}0.50$) argue for a genuine, power-modulated transition.
A Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 18/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 3.45 \times 10^{-11}$); sub-threshold $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
A systematic robustness analysis (1{,}160 configurations) confirms specification-invariance of the onset.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6 pairs per seed), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.

### 当前 discussion.tex 全文

```latex
\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Our claim is scoped to temporal predictive improvement~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}; bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders, and our cluster-adjusted FPR CI ($[0\%, 41\%]$; \S\ref{sec:limitations}) means true Type~I error may be non-negligible.

\paragraph{Non-confirming cells.}
Five of twenty phase-diagram cells show $0/8$ despite lying above the theoretical detection boundary: four are sync-dip cells ($\alpha{=}0.60$, $T{=}10$--$20$) and one is a boundary cell ($T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.45$).
The sync-dip dissolves by $T{=}25$ ($5/8$), confirming it is transient; its mechanism remains open---one hypothesis is synchronization between the replacement ratio and the model's internal mode dynamics.
Excluding these five cells, the remaining 15/15 match theory (LOO-CV MAE${=}0.037$).
Seed variance peaks at the onset boundary ($\alpha{=}0.50$: 6/8, 0/8, 6/8 across three seeds), consistent with a binary transition.

\paragraph{Metric-specific ceiling.}
Observed detection counts never exceed $6/8$: the 2/8 non-detected pairs involve MAUVE, whose floor saturation ($\mu{=}0.029$) eliminates the temporal gradient Granger precedence requires (\S\ref{sec:t20}); practitioners should prefer monotonically degrading metrics (e.g., distinct-$n$).

\paragraph{Cross-architecture failure modes.}
Five of fifteen conditions do not confirm forward detection (\S\ref{sec:generalization}): precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16: 0/8 vs fp32 6/8), bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43: reverse 6/8), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B: s42 2/8 vs s43 6/8), and architecture-specific decoupling (SmolLM3-3B entropy 0/4, violating mode amplification; Proposition~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}).
Phase-diagram replication at 1.4B confirms qualitatively preserved detection despite count attenuation (4--5/8; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}).

\paragraph{Entropy-diversity coupling.}
The entropy-diversity lag is structural: distinct-$n$ requires token mass to cross threshold~$\varepsilon$ ($\gamma$-margin; Proposition~\ref{prop:div_lag}), producing the ${\geq}1$-generation lag in 14/15 experiments; PermG's directional asymmetry (6/8 forward, 0/8 reverse) argues against a sensitivity artifact.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
WikiText yields exclusively forward PermG significance; C4 produces reverse 7/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}), indicating domain-dependent confounding.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
Longer $T$ lowers $\alpha_c$ sub-linearly (\S\ref{sec:theory}); PermG requires fp32 (bf16: 0/8 vs 6/8 in GPT-2).
Entropy is the optimal canary (14/15 cascade); triggered cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), bridging the detection-to-action gap that prior work leaves open.
```

### 当前 limitations.tex 全文

```latex
\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our landscape characterization uses Pythia-410M as the primary architecture; the phase diagram (\S\ref{sec:t20}) is Pythia-family-only (410M and 1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:scale_14b}), not cross-architecture.
Cross-architecture validation spans five families (345M--6.9B) but five of fifteen conditions do not confirm unambiguous directional detection (including GPT-2-medium s43 fp32, which shows bidirectional Granger significance despite clean directionality at s42), and frontier-scale behavior ($>$7B) is untested.
At 1.4B, entropy saturates within a single generation ($-27\%$ to $-39\%$ by gen~1), reducing temporal resolution and making MAUVE pairs systematically undetectable (floor $\mu{=}0.029$).
With $T{\leq}25$ observations, statistical power remains limited: since $\alpha_\infty{\approx}0$, longer observation windows should push $\alpha_c$ toward arbitrarily low contamination levels, but sub-linear signal growth ($\hat{\beta}{=}0.66$, CI $[0.24, 0.78]$) means diminishing returns; two of five methods (threshold onset, Toda--Yamamoto) are power-limited at these series lengths.
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ dissolves by $T{=}25$ but its mechanism---whether driven by numerical precision effects (bf16 yields 8/8), signal structure, or their interaction---remains open; boundary cells show substantial seed sensitivity (e.g., $T{=}10$, $\alpha{=}0.50$: 6/8, 0/8, 6/8 across three seeds).
All experiments use a single generation strategy (temperature~$1.0$, top-$k{=}50$); alternative decoding settings (nucleus sampling, lower temperature) may alter the collapse dynamics and detection landscape.
PermG's empirical FPR of $0/24$ yields a Clopper--Pearson 97.5\% upper bound of 14\%, but the three seeds are not independent (within-seed ICC${=}0.34$), widening the cluster-adjusted CI to $[0\%, 41\%]$; true FPR may be non-negligible.
```

We apply a max-split change-point test with bootstrap significance assessment ($n{=}5{,}000$, $p{<}0.05$) to each metric's generation-level time series ($T{=}11$).

Under the null control ($\alpha{=}0.00$, 3~seeds), downstream diversity metrics (distinct-1, distinct-2, distinct-3) produce significant change-points at generation~2 in all seeds (9/9 tests). With additional significant tests from ECE (2/3 seeds) and token entropy (1/3 seeds), the overall false positive rate reaches 66.7\% (12/18 tests; Table~\ref{tab:cp_null}). The monotonic drift inherent in iterative self-training is sufficient to trigger change-point detection even without canary contamination. Individual change-point significance therefore cannot serve as standalone evidence for a canary-specific effect.

Although individual significance is unreliable as a discriminator, the temporal ordering of detected change-points reverses between null and treatment conditions. In the null ($\alpha{=}0.00$), downstream metrics show the earliest significant breaks at generation~2 (all seeds), while significant canary breaks appear later (ECE at generations~4--8). Under treatment conditions ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), this ordering flips: canary metrics place their best splits at generation~1, followed by downstream diversity metrics at generations~2--4 and perplexity at generation~4 (Table~\ref{tab:cp_results}). This ordering reversal provides complementary evidence from a distinct statistical framework, consistent with the Granger-precedence analysis in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.
